payload.body: Phonetics is a human-made discipline of linguistics that studies the physical properties of speech sounds, as distinct from their systemic function within a particular language. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) domain: the object is the speech sound as a physical event — articulation (the configuration and movement of the articulators in producing it), acoustics (the pressure wave it generates), and perception (its auditory detection); the domain's boundary is the physical signal itself — the systemic organization of sound units into inventories and rules belongs to phonology, as the board's accepted morphology carve already assigns sound structure to phonology at the word's domain boundary; (2) method: analysis proceeds by measurement and cross-linguistic description — articulatory geometry, acoustic values such as formants and spectrograms, and perceptual classification — rather than by the contrastive inventory of any single language; (3) codification: findings are fixed in a shared apparatus independent of any one language — the International Phonetic Alphabet and its conventions, articulatory taxonomies (consonants by place and manner of articulation), and acoustic norms — which give phonetics its stable, reusable descriptive form. Phonetics persists as a discipline: it is taught as a field of linguistics, its categories (formant, place and manner of articulation, phoneme's physical realization) form the stable vocabulary of speech description across languages, and its apparatus is operationalized in speech synthesis and recognition, forensic phonetics, and the clinical assessment of speech.
